report:
The housing tenant challenge to the statutory exemption and unequal treatment centers on the legal status of the Bombay Housing Board (the Board) and its interaction with the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 (the Rent Act). The factual background establishes that the Sion Dharavi Camp was originally constructed and owned by the Government of India for military use during World War II [Sf0ec8991e3f5]. In 1948, the Government of Bombay purchased the camp and entrusted its management to the Bombay Provincial Housing Board, a body constituted by Government Resolution [S07a480fd64db]. Concurrently, the Bombay Housing Board was established as a body corporate under the Bombay Housing Board Act, 1948, competent to acquire and hold property [S07a480fd64db]. On June 1, 1949, following a necessary declaration by the Government of Bombay, the camp vested in the Board [Sea1c62736f22]. Prior to this vesting, the petitioner had occupied portions of the camp without authority or title, but an arrangement was made whereby he agreed to pay rent fixed by the Government of Bombay [Sea1c62736f22]. This agreement included provisions for repairs, with the petitioner’s rent initially set at Rs. 14 per month, later revised to Rs. 56-8 per month after reconditioning [S7fb6c9a94a27][Sbea8a25fb5b7].

The Board’s statutory scope is defined by the Bombay Housing Board Act, 1948. Section 3(3) of the Act deems the Board to be a 'local authority' specifically for the purposes of that Act and the Land Acquisition (Bombay Amendment) Act, 1948 [S5f96a5787509]. However, the central dispute arose when the Board served a notice to quit in February 1950, which the petitioner refused to comply with by not paying the revised rent [S425c649bee00]. In proceedings before the Court of Small Causes, the petitioner claimed protection under the Rent Act [S51643a81e6f4]. The Board countered that its premises were exempt from the Rent Act under Section 4, which states the Act does not apply to premises belonging to the Government or a local authority [S7c2bbc77f612][Se44560fe91e7]. The petitioner argued that the Board was not a 'local authority' within the meaning of Section 4 of the Rent Act and further contended that Section 4 violated Article 14 of the Constitution (equal protection) [Se9837a2f0396].

During the pendency of these proceedings, the legislature intervened via the Bombay Housing Board (Amendment) Act, 1951. This amendment introduced Section 3-A, which explicitly declared that the Rent Act shall not apply, nor shall be deemed to have ever applied, to land or buildings belonging to or vesting in the Board, or to tenancies created by the Board [Sd74eb1d0ec62][S928d0b11125e][S1e41f8665839]. This provision effectively bypassed the need to determine if the Board qualified as a 'local authority' under the original Section 4 by creating a specific statutory exemption for the Board.

Procedurally, the Trial Court held that the Board was a local authority under Section 4 of the Rent Act and that Section 4 did not contravene Article 14, granting possession to the Board [S808d8993dc70]. The High Court, however, found it difficult to classify the Board as a local authority but upheld the eviction based on the retrospective effect of the newly added Section 3-A, finding no infraction of Article 14 [S69838ebf5310][S44341cce9445]. The petitioner then sought special leave to appeal and filed a substantive petition under Article 32 of the Constitution [Sff6d93cc06d0][S149698b5d452]. Before the Supreme Court, the sole issue urged was whether Section 3-A offends the equal protection clause of Article 14 [S92c014602292].

Regarding comparator evidence, the petitioner’s counsel argued that numerous Co-operative Housing Societies in Bombay, incorporated under the Co-operative Societies Act and similarly situated in their objective to solve housing problems, are not exempted from the Rent Act [S3a4cb5d57469]. The petitioner posited that treating the Board differently from these societies violates Article 14, which guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws [Lb8acbb298b78]. The available record supports the existence of this differential treatment argument but does not contain the Supreme Court's final determination on whether this classification constitutes permissible legislative distinction or unconstitutional discrimination. The procedural posture remains that the lower courts accepted the validity of the exemption (either through 'local authority' status or the amended Act), while the constitutional challenge to the amended Act itself is the live issue before the apex court.
